Before anything else happens, your prompt gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**. A token can be a whole word, part of a word, or even just punctuation. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of these pieces, and each one gets swapped for an ID number.

Say you type "The cat sat." The model might see something like [464, 3797, 3332, 13]. (Those numbers are made up for illustration, since every tokenizer uses its own.)

replies.raw:
Right, C. The model works only with those numbers, never with letters or whole sentences.

Now for what it does with them. The model's core job is **next-token prediction**: given all the tokens so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next.

Take "The cat sat on the ___". Words like "mat", "floor" and "couch" would score high, while "democracy" would score close to zero.

[KEY]An LLM generates text by repeatedly predicting a likely next token, adding it to the text, and predicting again.[/KEY]

[EX]After "The cat sat on the", suppose the model scores "mat" highest. It picks a token, appends it, and then runs the whole process again on the longer text to choose the following token, one token at a time.[/EX]

This is why the model isn't looking up a stored answer the way a search engine would. It is building its reply piece by piece from likelihoods.

[Q]
A friend says, "ChatGPT just looks up the answer to your question in a giant database." Which response is most accurate?
A) It scores likely next tokens and builds its reply one token at a time, so there is no single stored answer being retrieved
B) It checks each token against a list of verified facts before writing it
C) It does look things up: it finds the closest stored answer and copies it out
ANS: A
[/Q]

The model only scores which token is *likely* to come next, based on patterns it absorbed from huge amounts of text. It has no built-in step that verifies truth, and that is exactly why AI can sound confident and still be wrong (we'll get to that in a later lesson).

So the accurate answer was A: it builds its reply one token at a time from likelihoods, with no stored answer being retrieved and no fact-checking step.

replies.user: [CURRICULUM: Unit 1, Lesson 1] Teach me what physically happens inside an LLM when I type a prompt. Start with tokenization and next-token prediction. After explaining, give me a hands-on exercise.
replies.raw:
Here's something that surprises most people: an LLM never sees your words. It only ever sees numbers.

Before your prompt goes anywhere, it gets chopped into pieces called **tokens**. A token is often a whole word, but it can also be part of a word or a piece of punctuation. GPT-4's tokenizer has a vocabulary of about 100,000 of them, and each one gets assigned a number.

Take the sentence "I sat on the bank of the river." The model gets a list of numbers, one per token, and nothing else. The word "bank" gets the same token whether you're talking about money or mud.

So how does the model know which meaning you intended? That's where the other words come in, and we'll get to that soon. First, let's check that the basic idea landed.

[CHECK]If you type "I put cash in the bank," what does the model actually receive before it does anything else: your words, or something different? Answer in your own words.[/CHECK]

replies.user: Got it — the model first breaks my sentence into tokens and turns them into numbers, because it can only work with numbers, not raw words. The split doesn't always match word boundaries.
replies.raw:
Spot on, and you added something I only hinted at: tokens don't always line up with whole words. A long or rare word might be split into several tokens, while a common word is usually just one.

Now for the second idea: what the model does with those numbers.

Its core job is **next-token prediction**. Given every token so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next. Then it picks one, adds it to the text, and repeats the whole process.

Try this one: "The cat sat on the ___". The model puts high probability on a few tokens like "mat" or "floor", and very little on "democracy". It isn't looking anything up.

It's weighing patterns it absorbed during training.

Compare that with "My favorite thing to do on weekends is ___". Far more words could plausibly fit, so the probability spreads out across many options.

One more detail: back to "bank". The model resolves "river" versus "cash" through a mechanism called attention, which lets each token weigh how relevant the other tokens are. That's what sorts out the meaning.

[CHECK]In your own words: why would the model be more confident about the next word in "The cat sat on the ___" than in "My favorite thing to do on weekends is ___"?[/CHECK]

[Q]
Which statement best describes what the model works with after you hit send?
A) It looks up your sentence in a database of stored answers
B) It reads your words as a human would, one letter at a time
C) It converts your text into tokens, and each token becomes a number

replies.user: I picked C) It converts your text into tokens, and each token becomes a number
replies.raw:
Right, and notice what that rules out. The model isn't searching a database for a stored answer, because all it ever receives is those numbers.

So what does it do with them? It plays one game, over and over: **next-token prediction**. Given every token so far, it scores every token in its vocabulary by how likely it is to come next.

Take "The cat sat on the ___". Words like "mat", "floor" or "couch" would score high, while "democracy" would score near zero. The model picks from the high scorers, adds that token to the text, then repeats the whole process for the next one.

That's how a full answer gets built: one token at a time, each chosen based on everything before it.

[KEY]An LLM writes by repeatedly scoring every possible next token and picking from the likeliest ones.[/KEY]
